record.tranche_reason: Trains language models at multiple sizes and measures validation cross-entropy against training compute, directly extending the scaling measurement on new runs.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports many downstream-task scores, but only aggregate or explicitly described scale trends are recorded here; individual benchmark scores are not evidence about held-out pretraining loss. Architecture sensitivity is mentioned with reference to prior work, not tested here.
record.test_reason: The authors train 8 GPT-3 sizes plus 6 extra-small models and plot validation cross-entropy against training compute (Fig. 3.1). They say the trend extends the Kaplan et al. power law by two orders of magnitude. They also report downstream accuracy across all 8 sizes.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors say the loss power law largely continues over two more orders of magnitude, with a possible slight bend. They report relatively smooth downstream gains for many, but explicitly not all, tasks, and describe 'roughly predictable trends of scaling in performance'.
record.recipe_differences: Measures autoregressive language-model validation loss across newly trained model sizes; all models use 300 billion training tokens, and the paper describes scaling with compute rather than independently varying parameters, tokens, and compute.

fits_no_version.finding: Human accuracy at spotting model-written news articles falls with model size; the authors fit a power law (86% control vs 52% for 175B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The human-perceived quality of generated text improves as a power law in model size.

record.problems: The loss-scaling evidence is presented in a figure and qualitative description rather than a table of loss values or fitted exponents. All models use the same stated training-token total, so token-count scaling is not independently tested. The downstream aggregate trend does not establish predictions from pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed model-by-model downstream scores and additional task-specific scaling results in Appendix H and the task sections are not individually transcribed; the selected rows capture the reported aggregate trends and the explicitly described shallow PIQA scaling.

untested.parts: Parameter and token axes separately. All models get 300B tokens, so only the compute-efficient frontier is shown, and no exponent is reported.
No new fit on small runs and no numeric loss prediction for the large runs; the evidence is the plotted continuation of the prior law.
Predicting downstream performance from pretraining loss. The paper asserts a link but does not analyse it.

missing.what: Arithmetic few-shot accuracy by size: 2D+ is 55.5 at 13B vs 100.0 at 175B, and 4D+ is 0.40 vs 25.5. This is a sharp, not smooth, jump.
ANLI accuracy is ~33% (chance) for all models below 175B, even few-shot; 175B reaches 40.2 on R3 few-shot. RTE: only 175B is convincingly above random.
WiC stays near 50% at all sizes (175B few-shot 55.3; zero-shot 0.00 for every size). Reversed words are ~0% at all sizes.
The authors note that a slight bending of the loss curve may be detectable.

record.verdict_notes: Jared Kaplan is a co-author, but this paper is not one of the original sources. The compute axis mixes model size with a fixed 300B tokens, and embedding parameters are excluded from the counts in Fig. 3.1. The possible slight bend in the loss curve is weak evidence for the V7 bending clause, too tentative to label. The V6 limits_scope verdict for arithmetic, NLI, WiC and reversed words rests on the text and Table H.1, not on any row.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports loss scaling with compute while training all models for 300 billion tokens; it does not independently sweep token count or establish parameter-count scaling with the other factors held non-bottlenecking.
The paper tests continuation of the loss trend to larger runs, but does not report a new fit on small runs with numerical predictions for specific larger-run losses.
No fixed-compute-budget search for loss-minimising parameter and token allocations.
Architecture details vary across sizes, but the paper does not isolate architecture effects at fixed parameter count.
No tests of other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling laws.
Reports downstream performance trends with model size, not predictions of downstream performance from fitted pretraining loss.
Does not systematically vary parameter counting, schedule, data, or fitting method to test whether exponents or compute-optimal allocations depend on setup.

rows.subject: GPT-3 model series, including 6 extra-small models
rows.size_stated: 8 models from 125 million to 175 billion parameters; Figure 3.1 also includes 6 extra-small models with as few as 100,000 parameters
rows.operation_detail: Measured validation cross-entropy loss across models trained at different sizes and compute levels.

conditions.value: varied; training compute described as making efficient use of compute
125 million to 175 billion; Figure 3.1 extends down to 100,000 parameters

rows.value: The loss follows a power-law trend with training compute; the trend extends by two more orders of magnitude with only small deviations from the predicted curve.
rows.note: The figure includes the 8 trained models and 6 extra-small models. The paper says parameter counts and compute exclude embedding parameters for this figure.
rows.check: The value is correct. It omits the authors' caveat that 'a slight bending of the curve can perhaps be detected' (Sec. 7). The 'predicted curve' is the Kaplan et al. law extended to larger runs, which bears on V2 extrapolation.

relationships.condition: Arithmetic, NLI (ANLI, RTE), WiC, reversed words
relationships.reason: From the text, not rows. Arithmetic jumps sharply from 13B to 175B; models below 175B sit at chance on ANLI and RTE; WiC and reversed words stay near chance at every size.
relationships.display_finding: Arithmetic improves sharply from 13B to 175B, while ANLI and RTE remain at chance below 175B; WiC and word reversal remain near chance across all sizes.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Arithmetic, NLI (ANLI, RTE), WiC, reversed words
source_check.reason: This group needs separate verdicts. Retain limits_scope for abrupt arithmetic and NLI gains concentrated at 175B. Assign challenges to WiC and reversed words: Section 3.7 reports chance-level WiC performance despite alternative formulations, and Section 3.9.2 explicitly states that none of the models can reverse words. These are absent effects, not merely incomplete gains.
